Topic: Pure Fourier Series: The Power of Symmetry

Target audience: University Engineering and Mathematics Students

Section: section_1 — The Hook: The Whistle-Bot's Pure Tones

Lecture lines:
Meet Whistle-Bot, a master of pure periodic tones.
Most sounds are messy, but Whistle-Bot prefers smooth oscillations.
He moves in a jerky, jagged square wave pattern.
Can we recreate this jump using only smooth movements?
Let's explore the power of mathematical symmetry.

Planned animations:
Whistle-Bot moves in a jerky square pattern (#FFD700).
A single smooth Sine wave appears (#ADD8E6).
Whistle-Bot's path is overlaid with the Sine wave.
Second harmonic Sine wave joins the sum (#90EE90).
Resulting wave starts looking like the square path.

Section: section_2 — Prerequisite: The Full Fourier Recipe

Lecture lines:
Every periodic function is a mathematical "stew" of waves.
The recipe includes constants, cosines, and sine components.
These building blocks are independent and do not mix.

Planned animations:
Full Fourier formula appears in the center (#FFFFFF).
Highlight a0 in yellow (#FFFF00).
Highlight Cosine terms in blue (#0000FF).
Highlight Sine terms in green (#00FF00).
Icons for Sine and Cosine remain separate (Orthogonality).

Section: section_3 — The Symmetry Filter: Even and Odd Functions

Lecture lines:
Symmetry simplifies our mathematical "stew" significantly.
Even functions mirror perfectly across the vertical axis.
Odd functions exhibit rotational symmetry through the origin.
Cosines are the "Even Kings" of the wave world.
Sines serve as the "Odd Queens" in our series.

Planned animations:
Parabola y=x^2 mirrors across the Y-axis (#ADD8E6).
Cubic y=x^3 rotates 180 degrees through origin (#90EE90).
'Even King' Cosine graph flashes on the left (#ADD8E6).
'Odd Queen' Sine graph flashes on the right (#90EE90).

Section: section_4 — Deriving the Pure Sine Series

Lecture lines:
For odd functions, all cosine terms vanish to zero.
We are left with a pure sine series representation.
Integration only requires half the period, then double it.

Planned animations:
Odd Square Wave enters a 'Cosine Filter' box (#FFFFFF).
Cosine terms (an) are ejected from the filter (#FF0000).
an = 0 text appears in bold (#FF0000).
Formula for bn fades in with 2/L highlighted (#FFFF00).

Section: section_5 — Deriving the Pure Cosine Series

Lecture lines:
For even functions, all sine terms disappear completely.
This creates a pure cosine series for the function.
The constant average value, a0, remains an even component.

Planned animations:
Even Triangle Wave enters a 'Sine Filter' box (#FFFFFF).
Sine terms (bn) are ejected from the filter (#FF0000).
bn = 0 text appears in bold (#FF0000).
a0 (average value) stays with the Cosine terms (#FFFF00).

Section: section_6 — Application: Building the Square Wave

Lecture lines:
Let's build a square wave using our sine series.
Adding the first harmonic creates a basic smooth curve.
Higher odd harmonics sharpen the corners of the wave.
With enough terms, a jagged square shape emerges.
Watch the "ears" appear at the edges—the Gibbs Phenomenon.

Planned animations:
Plot y = sin(x) (fundamental frequency) (#ADD8E6).
Add y = 1/3 sin(3x) to the graph (#90EE90).
Add y = 1/5 sin(5x) to the graph (#FFFF00).
Highlight the 'ripples' near the jump (Gibbs Phenomenon).

Section: section_7 — Summary: Efficiency through Geometry

Lecture lines:
Pure series exploit the inherent symmetry of physical systems.
Symmetry reduces our computational work by half.
Elegant geometry makes complex math much more efficient.

Planned animations:
Left: Complex formula vs Right: Simple formula (#FFFFFF).
'50% Less Math' label appears on the right (#00FF00).
A vibrating string animation shows physical symmetry (#ADD8E6).
Closing text: 'Symmetry is efficiency' (#FFFFFF).
